title: SUBSTRING/LEFT vs. LIKE Prefix
description: SUBSTRING(col,1,n) in a WHERE clause can't use an index; an anchored LIKE 'prefix%' does the same test with a seek. Why it matters: prefix searches (SKUs, codes, names) are a common pattern, and knowing the sargable rewrite is the difference between a fast lookup and a full scan.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson covers one more common way developers accidentally disable an index: using `SUBSTRING()` or `LEFT()` to check just part of a text value, like the first four characters of a product code, instead of using a prefix-matching `LIKE` pattern.

Why does this happen? `SUBSTRING(Sku, 1, 4) = 'ELEC'` creates a brand-new, computed 4-character string for every row before comparing it. That computed value doesn't exist in the index — the index stores the *full* `Sku` values, sorted alphabetically. To check the computed substring, SQL Server has to slice every row's value first, which means visiting every row one at a time instead of jumping through the sorted index.

Think back to the phone-book analogy: the book is sorted by full name, so you can jump straight to "Smith." But if someone insists on trimming each entry down to just its first four letters before comparing — checking "does the trimmed version say S-M-I-T?" — that trimming step has to happen for every single entry, because the phone book was never organized by "first four letters," it was organized by full name (which happens to *start* the same way). The fix is to rewrite the check as a prefix search instead — `WHERE Sku LIKE 'ELEC%'` — which SQL Server can match directly against the sorted index, the same way it would find "Smith" by jumping to the S section.

## Scenario
A catalog screen filters products by their category prefix (the first four characters of the `Sku`) with `WHERE SUBSTRING(Sku, 1, 4) = 'ELEC'`. `Sku` is indexed, yet the query scans every row.

## Why it's slow
Wrapping the column in `SUBSTRING(Sku, 1, 4)` produces a **computed value**. SQL Server cannot match a computed value against the raw index key, so the `IX_Products_Sku` index can only be **scanned**, not seeked — logical reads grow with the whole table.

## What to look for
- An **Index Scan** on `Products` reading all rows.
- Logical reads far larger than the ~10,000 matching rows warrant.

## The fix
A prefix match is naturally a **range**: every `Sku` that starts with `'ELEC'` sits together in the index. `WHERE Sku LIKE 'ELEC%'` is **sargable** — SQL Server seeks to the start of the `'ELEC'` range and reads only those rows. (Note: a **leading** wildcard like `LIKE '%ELEC'` is *not* sargable — only a trailing one is.)
startingQuery: SELECT ProductId, Sku, Name FROM Products WHERE SUBSTRING(Sku, 1, 4) = 'ELEC';
hints: Look at the operator on Products — is it a Scan or a Seek? SUBSTRING(Sku,1,4) forces a Scan.
A function on the column makes the predicate non-sargable: the index key is the raw Sku, not SUBSTRING(Sku,1,4).
A prefix is a range. Rewrite it as WHERE Sku LIKE 'ELEC%' so the index can seek.
